fields.meta_title: Telemedicine Consent Form Builder for Clinics | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a telemedicine consent form that checks the patient's state at every visit, saves a callback number and asks about recording on its own line.
fields.h1: Build a Telemedicine Consent Form for Every Virtual Visit
fields.hero_description: Tell Emergent how your clinic runs video and phone visits. It builds a telemedicine consent form that captures where the patient is, how to reach them and their answer on recording.
fields.features_subheading: The questions an exam room never had to ask, answered before the video opens.
fields.feature_1:
The patient's state, asked at every check-in

Ask which state the patient is in each time they join, not once at intake. A state outside the clinician's license list holds the visit and alerts the clinician before it opens.
fields.feature_2:
A callback number for the dropped call

Collect the address where the patient is today and a number to call if the video fails. Both sit on the visit screen beside the video, ready if the clinician has to phone back.
fields.feature_3:
Recording consent on a separate line

Ask about recording as its own yes or no, apart from consent to treatment. A no marks every session for that patient as do not record on the clinician's schedule until it changes.
fields.feature_4:
Visit types the patient agreed to

List each way your clinic sees patients remotely and let the patient tick the ones they accept. The scheduler then offers only those visit types when the front desk books.
fields.feature_5:
Every signed version kept with its date

Send the form again when your wording changes or a renewal date arrives. Each signed version stays on the patient's record with its date, beside the one signed most recently.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can run inside your patient portal

Export the full source to your GitHub repository. Your developers can host the consent form inside your patient portal and keep changing it there, with no rebuild from scratch.

fields.tab_content_1:
Checked in from Idaho, held for the therapist

Juniper Counseling's therapists see clients only in the states where they hold licenses, Oregon and Washington. Each check-in asks where the client is today. Eli Marsh opens his 4 p.m. session link from Boise, Idaho. The session stays closed, and therapist Dana Ruiz gets an alert before it starts.
fields.tab_content_2:
Video froze at 10:14 and the doctor called back

Cedar Ridge asks every patient for their current street address and a callback number before the video opens. Ruth Okafor's video freezes at 10:14 a.m. during a visit about a rash. Dr. Ben Hale sees her number beside the frozen frame, calls her, and finishes the visit by phone.
fields.tab_content_3:
Recording gets its own yes or no

Supervisors at Maple Hall Training Clinic review recorded sessions with student clinicians. The form asks about treatment and recording on separate lines. A client can accept treatment and decline recording. This week 3 of 12 clients said no to recording, and their sessions show Do not record.
fields.tab_content_4:
A phone-only patient never lands in a video slot

Sam Porter agreed to phone visits only on Pinecrest Health's consent form. When the front desk tries to book his follow-up as a video visit, the scheduler stops the booking and offers the next phone slot, Thursday at 2:30 p.m. The receptionist books it without calling him first.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Telemedicine Consent Form
fields.howto_description: Start with the questions a video visit raises that an exam room never did. The build itself is the short part.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Gather the consent you use now
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Ask for the state at every visit
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write the plan for a dropped call
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Keep recording on its own line
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pull together the telehealth consent each clinician uses today, whether it is a PDF, a paragraph in your intake packet or a script read aloud. Mark where two clinicians describe the same risk in different words, and settle those first.
fields.howto_step_2_des: HHS telehealth guidance, checked in October 2026, says a clinician must be licensed or legally permitted to practice in the state where the patient is located. Ask for that state at each check-in, and give the form each clinician's list of states.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Decide what happens when the video fails: who calls whom, on which number, and when the visit moves to the phone. Collect the patient's address and a callback number at check-in, plus the local emergency numbers your plan relies on.
fields.howto_step_4_des: If a session might be recorded or watched by a supervisor, ask about it apart from consent to treatment. HHS guidance says to tell the patient when anyone is observing and get their consent at the start. Store the answer where schedulers see it.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your wording, your clinicians' license states and your visit types into Emergent. It builds the form, the check-in screen and a table of signed consents. Ask for changes in plain English, such as a Spanish version or a parent signature for minors.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Link the form to your scheduling or video tool through its API. Each booking then carries the patient's accepted visit types and recording answer, and every check-in writes the patient's state and callback number to the visit record.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Test it, then have it reviewed
fields.howto_step_7_des: Run one test check-in from a covered state and one from a state outside the list, then try a booking that breaks a phone-only choice. Ask a healthcare attorney in your state to review the consent language before any patient signs it.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is nine clinic PDFs, each a page of I-understand clauses and one signature line. None records where the patient is sitting when the visit starts, what happens when the video freezes, or whether the patient agreed to be recorded. This page lays out what a virtual-visit consent has to capture, then shows four telehealth settings using it: a therapy practice that checks the client's state at check-in, a family clinic with a callback number on screen when a call drops, a training clinic that asks about recording on its own line, and a patient who agreed to phone visits only.
tab_stories: Juniper Counseling's therapists hold licenses in Oregon and Washington, so when Eli Marsh checks in from Boise, Idaho, the session is held and therapist Dana Ruiz gets an alert before the call opens.

At Cedar Ridge Family Medicine the check-in saves the street address the patient is at and a callback number, so when Ruth Okafor's video freezes at 10:14 a.m., Dr. Ben Hale calls her back on that number.

Maple Hall Training Clinic records sessions for supervision, asks about recording on a separate line from treatment, and the 3 of 12 clients who said no show as do not record on the student clinicians' schedule.

claims_to_source: Telemedicine refers specifically to remote clinical services; telehealth is broader and can include non-clinical services such as patient health education, social support and medication adherence
Providers must be licensed or legally permitted to practice in the state where the patient is located, and should verify the patient's location before an appointment

Providers may be required to obtain informed consent for telehealth, laws vary by state, and consent can be documented in writing or electronically before the visit or verbally at the start of each session
If anyone is observing a telehealth visit, the provider should tell the patient and get consent at the start
A telehealth emergency plan confirms the address where the patient is at the start of each visit and lists local emergency numbers near the patient
Most states require official informed consent before treatment by telehealth for behavioral health
